title: Catheters and Catheterisation
path: Nursing Care of Patients with Feeding and Elimination Problems

headings.title: Introduction to Catheters and Urinary Elimination
headings.content: Urinary elimination is a fundamental physiological process vital for maintaining fluid and electrolyte balance, eliminating metabolic waste, and preserving overall homeostasis in the human body. When this intricate process is compromised due to surgery, trauma, neurological impairment, or severe illness, alternative interventions become necessary. Urinary catheterisation is a core nursing procedure taught to nursing students in Nigeria, involving the insertion of a hollow, flexible tube through the urethra into the urinary bladder to drain urine. As a nursing professional, understanding the core principles of urinary elimination allows you to identify when normal voiding fails and recognize the clinical indicators that necessitate mechanical drainage. Catheters act as a bridge to restore or monitor urine output when patients cannot do so independently. However, because inserting a foreign object into the sterile urinary tract introduces significant infection risks, it must be performed with rigorous aseptic technique and strict clinical indications. Mastery of catheterisation not only aids in immediate patient comfort and output monitoring but also prevents long-term renal damage, urinary stasis, and severe systemic infections. By grasping the foundation of urinary elimination, student nurses can appreciate why meticulous care and prompt removal of catheters are among the most critical responsibilities in clinical practice.

headings.title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Urinary Tract
headings.content: A comprehensive understanding of the genitourinary system is essential for safe and successful catheterisation. The urinary tract consists of two kidneys, two ureters, the urinary bladder, and the urethra. Urine produced in the kidneys travels down the ureters to the muscular reservoir known as the bladder, where it is stored until micturition occurs. The bladder wall is composed of the detrusor muscle, which relaxes to allow bladder filling and contracts to expel urine during voiding. The exit from the bladder is controlled by internal and external urethral sphincters, which regulate urinary continence. The anatomy of the urethra differs significantly between males and females, a vital clinical distinction for nursing students. The female urethra is relatively short, measuring approximately 3.7 to 6.2 centimeters, and opens straight into the perineum between the clitoris and vaginal opening, making it more prone to ascending bacterial colonization. Conversely, the male urethra is much longer, measuring about 18 to 20 centimeters, and features anatomical curves including the prostatic, membranous, and spongy (penile) sections. Passing a catheter through the longer male urethra requires careful maneuvering through these curves to avoid trauma to the delicate mucosal lining. Knowledge of these structural differences directly influences how nurses position patients, select catheter sizes, and advance the tubing smoothly into the bladder without causing injury.

headings.title: Types of Urinary Catheters and Equipment
headings.content: Urinary catheters and associated equipment vary widely based on clinical needs, duration of use, and patient anatomy. Catheters are generally classified as intermittent or indwelling. Intermittent catheters (often called straight catheters) are single-lumen tubes inserted to drain the bladder and immediately removed once drainage is complete, making them ideal for patients with neurogenic bladder or chronic urinary retention who perform self-catheterisation. Indwelling retention catheters (commonly known as Foley catheters) feature a dual-lumen or triple-lumen design. One lumen allows urine drainage, a second lumen is used to inflate a retention balloon with sterile water to keep the catheter secured in the bladder, and a third lumen (if present) facilitates continuous bladder irrigation. Catheters are manufactured from various materials such as latex, silicone, and Teflon-coated latex. Silicone is often preferred for long-term use due to its biocompatibility and resistance to encrustation, while latex may cause allergic reactions in sensitive patients. Equipment needed for the procedure typically includes a sterile catheterisation tray, antiseptic cleansing solution, sterile gloves, water-soluble lubricating jelly, a drainage bag, and securement devices. Selecting the appropriate catheter French (Fr) size—typically 14 Fr to 16 Fr for average adult females and 16 Fr to 18 Fr for adult males—ensures effective drainage while minimizing urethral trauma.

headings.title: Indications for Catheterisation
headings.content: Catheterisation is an invasive clinical procedure that should only be performed when specific medical indications are present. Inappropriate or routine use of indwelling catheters significantly increases the risk of catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs) and patient morbidity. Standard indications for urinary catheterisation include the management of acute urinary retention or bladder outlet obstruction, such as from benign prostatic hyperplasia or severe blood clots. Catheters are also essential for accurate hourly monitoring of urine output in critically ill patients in intensive care units or during major surgical procedures where fluid balance must be closely titrated. Other valid indications include facilitating healing of open sacral or perineal wounds in incontinent patients, managing chronic urinary retention when intermittent catheterisation is impractical, performing urodynamic studies, and providing comfort measures for terminally ill patients where bed linen changes cause severe distress. Nurses must critically evaluate every physician order for catheterisation against these evidence-based indications. If an order lacks a clear clinical justification, the nurse has a professional obligation to question the order and discuss alternatives with the healthcare team, thereby safeguarding the patient from unnecessary complications and promoting safe, patient-centered nursing care in Nigerian health facilities.

headings.title: Pre-Procedural Assessment and Preparation
headings.content: Thorough pre-procedural assessment and preparation are critical prerequisites for successful and safe catheterisation. Before initiating the procedure, the nurse must review the patient's medical record for clinical indications, known allergies (such as latex, iodine, or specific lubricants), history of previous urological surgeries, and anatomical anomalies. The nurse should explain the procedure clearly to the patient or legal guardian to alleviate anxiety, gain informed consent, and ensure cooperation. Assessing the patient's last voiding time, bladder fullness through abdominal palpation or bladder scanner, and baseline vital signs provides important clinical context. Preparation of the environment involves ensuring adequate lighting, privacy screens, and a clean working surface. Positioning the patient correctly is paramount: female patients are typically placed in the dorsal recumbent position with knees flexed and feet apart (or Sims position as an alternative), while male patients are placed in a standard supine position with legs extended. Gathering and checking all equipment beforehand—ensuring the sterile tray is intact, the light source is functional, and the correct catheter size is available—prevents breaks in sterile technique during the procedure. Proper hand hygiene and donning personal protective equipment (PPE) set the stage for maintaining a strict sterile field throughout catheter insertion.

headings.title: Step-by-Step Procedure for Male and Female Catheterisation
headings.content: Performing catheterisation requires strict adherence to sterile technique and gentle handling of urological tissues. Begin by setting up the sterile field, donning sterile gloves, and arranging equipment. For female catheterisation, use your non-dominant hand to separate the labia minora to clearly visualize the urethral meatus, treating this hand as contaminated once touched. Cleanse the meatus from front to back (clitoris toward the anus) using antiseptic swabs, using a fresh swab for each stroke. Lubricate the catheter tip (5 to 7 centimeters for females), gently insert it into the urethra until urine begins to flow, and then advance it another 2 to 5 centimeters to ensure the balloon is fully inside the bladder before inflation. For male catheterisation, hold the penis at a 90-degree angle to the body, retract the foreshut (if uncircumcised), and cleanse the glans in a circular motion from the meatus outward. Apply generous water-soluble lubricant (15 to 20 centimeters into the urethra if using a syringe applicator) to ease passage. Straighten the penis to a 45-to-60-degree angle, insert the catheter smoothly through the urethra past the prostate gland into the bladder until urine flows, and advance it to the bifurcation. Inflate the retention balloon with the prescribed volume of sterile water, gently pull back until resistance is felt to ensure secure placement, connect the drainage system, and secure the tubing to the thigh or lower abdomen to prevent urethral traction.

headings.title: Ongoing Catheter Care and Maintenance
headings.content: Ongoing care and maintenance of an indwelling urinary catheter are essential nursing responsibilities focused on preventing catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs) and maintaining unobstructed urine flow. The cornerstone of catheter maintenance is upholding a closed drainage system; breaking this seal introduces bacteria directly into the bladder. The drainage bag must always be kept below the level of the patient's bladder at all times to prevent the backflow of urine, which can cause ascending infections. The tubing and bag should be secured to the patient's thigh (for females) or lower abdomen/anterior thigh (for males) using specialized securement devices to eliminate traction on the bladder neck and urethral meatus, which can otherwise cause pain, bleeding, and tissue necrosis. Routine perineal hygiene should be performed daily and after bowel movements using mild soap and warm water, gently cleansing away from the meatus. Nurses must monitor and document urine output characteristics, including volume, color, clarity, and odor, reporting any cloudiness, hematuria, or sediment immediately. Routine prophylactic irrigation is not recommended, but if irrigation is ordered to clear obstruction, strict aseptic technique must be maintained. Encouraging adequate oral fluid intake (unless contraindicated) helps naturally flush the urinary tract and prevents sediment buildup.

headings.title: Potential Complications and Nursing Interventions
headings.content: Despite careful insertion and maintenance, urinary catheterisation carries risks of various complications that require vigilant monitoring and prompt nursing intervention. The most prevalent complication is a catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI), signaled by fever, chills, suprapubic tenderness, cloudy urine, and foul odor. Nursing interventions for CAUTI include notifying the physician, obtaining a sterile urine sample through the port (never from the bag), and administering prescribed antibiotics. Another frequent issue is mechanical obstruction or urine bypass (leaking around the catheter), which can result from blood clots, sediment, kinks in the tubing, or bladder spasms. Nurses should inspect the system for kinks, flush gently if ordered, and administer antispasmodic medications like oxybutynin for bladder spasms. Urethral trauma, bleeding, and false passage creation can occur during difficult insertions; if resistance is encountered, the nurse must stop immediately rather than forcing the catheter. Accidental or premature removal by confused patients can cause severe urethral tearing; using mitts, behavioral interventions, or obtaining prompt medical review is vital. Long-term indwelling catheter use can also lead to chronic urethral erosion, hypospadias, and encrustation. Recognizing these complications early allows nurses to implement corrective measures and advocate for timely catheter removal.

headings.title: Catheter Removal Protocol
headings.content: The catheter removal protocol is a structured nursing procedure that marks the transition back to independent urinary elimination. A catheter should be removed as soon as it is no longer clinically indicated to minimize the risk of infection. To prepare, explain the procedure to the patient and reassure them that removal is generally quick and only causes minimal discomfort. Assemble clean gloves, a waterproof underpad, and a sterile syringe sized to match the inflation volume (usually 10 mL). Position the patient comfortably, place the underpad underneath them, and expose the perineal area. Insert the syringe hub completely into the inflation port (balloon port) and allow the sterile water to withdraw passively via vacuum, or gently aspirate to ensure all fluid is removed from the balloon. Never cut the catheter tubing to deflate the balloon, as this can leave a sharp edge or fail to deflate safely. Once the balloon is fully deflated, instruct the patient to take a deep breath and relax, then gently and smoothly withdraw the catheter along the natural curvature of the urethra. After removal, clean the perineal area and document the time of removal. The nurse must monitor the patient's subsequent voiding pattern closely, instructing them to report the first void. Post-removal urinary retention, burning, and frequency are common; nurses should measure the first void volume and use a bladder scanner or perform straight catheterisation if the patient is unable to void within 6 to 8 hours.
